claims.claim: Direct Lake on OneLake never falls back; Direct Lake on SQL falls back to DirectQuery for SQL views and SQL-based granular access control; framing copies metadata in seconds; guardrails per SKU table.
Direct Lake behavior values Automatic (default), DirectLakeOnly and DirectQueryOnly; framing can fail when a table exceeds guardrails.

concept_html:
Direct Lake lets a semantic model read Delta tables in OneLake directly, loading only the columns a query needs into memory. It combines Import-like query speed with no copy of the data. A refresh does not reload data. It performs framing: it records which Delta table versions the model uses. Framing takes seconds, and afterwards queries see the data as of that frame. Automatic updates, a schedule or an API call can trigger framing.

There are two kinds (Microsoft Learn, updated September 2026):

  • Direct Lake on OneLake reads Delta tables from one or more Fabric items. It never falls back to DirectQuery. If it cannot load data, the query fails.
  • Direct Lake on SQL analytics endpoints reads one Fabric item through its endpoint. When it cannot load a table directly, it falls back to DirectQuery: for example when the table is a SQL view, or when the warehouse uses SQL-based granular access control. Fallback queries are slower.

The model property Direct Lake behavior controls fallback for the SQL kind:

  • Automatic (default): silently fall back to DirectQuery. Reports keep working, more slowly.
  • DirectLakeOnly: fail with an error instead. Use it in development to find fallbacks.
  • DirectQueryOnly: always use DirectQuery, to measure the difference.

Guardrails depend on the SKU. For each table, Fabric limits Parquet files, row groups and rows. Over a guardrail, framing can fail (or, on the SQL kind, queries fall back). From Learn's table:

SKU Parquet files per table Rows per table Max memory
F2 to F32 1,000 300 million 3 to 10 GB
F64 5,000 1.5 billion 25 GB
F512 and above 10,000 12 to 24 billion 200 to 400 GB

Small files hit the file guardrail first. Compact gold tables with OPTIMIZE (lesson A3-L3), and give Direct Lake tables V-Order (lesson C5-L2).

SMALL = (1000, 300)
GUARDRAILS: dict[str, tuple[int, float]] = {
    "F2": SMALL, "F4": SMALL, "F8": SMALL, "F16": SMALL, "F32": SMALL,
    "F64": (5000, 1500), "F128": (5000, 3000), "F256": (5000, 6000),
}


def guardrail_problems(sku: str, parquet_files: int, rows_millions: float) -> list[str]:
    """Direct Lake per-table guardrails a table exceeds on a SKU.

    Raises:
        KeyError: For a SKU not in the table.
    """
    max_files, max_rows = GUARDRAILS[sku]
    problems = []
    if parquet_files > max_files:
        problems.append("files")
    if rows_millions > max_rows:
        problems.append("rows")
    return problems

from pyspark.sql import DataFrame


def publish_hourly(df: DataFrame, table: str) -> None:
    """Append the latest hour, then compact small files for Direct Lake."""
    df.repartition(1).write.mode("append").saveAsTable(table)
    df.sparkSession.sql(f"OPTIMIZE {table}")
    return None

title: Direct Lake, framing and the fallback you did not plan
why_html: A sales model on an F32 capacity was fast in testing. After six months of hourly appends, the fact table held 2,400 small Parquet files, above the F32 guardrail of 1,000. The model used Direct Lake on the SQL endpoint with the Automatic behaviour, so queries quietly fell back to DirectQuery. Reports took 40 seconds instead of two. Nobody saw an error. A nightly OPTIMIZE kept the table at a few dozen files and restored Direct Lake.
